claim: Humans form social coalitions in every society.
source: Humans form social coalitions in every society, yet we know little about how we learn and represent social group boundaries.
evidence: This is a general statement presented in the abstract without specific supporting data or citations in this sentence.

claim: We know little about how we learn and represent social group boundaries.
source: Humans form social coalitions in every society, yet we know little about how we learn and represent social group boundaries.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, presented as background.

claim: Trial-by-trial estimates of 'allyship' based on dyadic similarity between participants and each agent recruited medial prefrontal cortex/pregenual anterior cingulate (pgACC).
source: Trial-by-trial estimates of 'allyship' based on dyadic similarity between participants and each agent recruited medial prefrontal cortex/pregenual anterior cingulate (pgACC).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Latent social group structure-based allyship estimates recruited right anterior insula (rAI).
source: Latent social group structure-based allyship estimates, in contrast, recruited right anterior insula (rAI).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Variability in the brain signal from rAI improved prediction of variability in ally-choice behavior.
source: Variability in the brain signal from rAI improved prediction of variability in ally-choice behavior, whereas variability from the pgACC did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of neural signal and behavioral data.

claim: Variability from the pgACC did not improve prediction of variability in ally-choice behavior.
source: Variability in the brain signal from rAI improved prediction of variability in ally-choice behavior, whereas variability from the pgACC did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant improvement.

claim: Being able to distinguish 'us' from 'them' is a core social capacity.
source: Being able to distinguish 'us' from 'them' is a core social capacity (Brown, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown, 1991.

claim: We know surprisingly little about how social group boundaries are learned and represented in the brain—particularly in the absence of overt cues to individuals' group membership.
source: Yet we know surprisingly little about how social group boundaries are learned and represented in the brain—particularly in the absence of overt cues to individuals' group membership.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: People use judgments of similarity to one's self on some contextually relevant feature (e.g., skin tone) to distinguish in-group from out-group members.
source: One dominant account is that people use judgments of similarity to one's self on some contextually relevant feature (e.g., skin tone).
evidence: This describes a dominant theoretical account in the field.

claim: Neuroimaging studies have attempted to identify an overlap between brain regions associated with self-referential processes and categorization of others as in-group members.
source: Accordingly, neuroimaging studies have attempted to identify an overlap between brain regions associated with self-referential processes and categorization of others as in-group members (Molenberghs and Morrison, 2014; Morrison et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: A ventral region of medial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), including pregenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC), is reliably associated with thinking about one's own and similar others' traits, mental states, and characteristics.
source: A ventral region of medial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), including pregenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC), is reliably associated with thinking about one's own and similar others' traits, mental states, and characteristics (Cikara et al., 2014; Heleven and Van Overwalle, 2016; Jenkins et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: People may rely on functional relations between one's self and a target (e.g., 'Are you with me or against me?') rather than prioritizing similarity to oneself.
source: Rather than prioritizing similarity to oneself, people may rely on functional relations between one's self and a target (e.g., 'Are you with me or against me?'; Cikara and Fiske, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cikara and Fiske, 2013.

claim: Social group dynamics may be better captured by a model that integrates information about how agents relate to one another in addition to oneself.
source: However, social group dynamics may be better captured by a model that integrates information about how agents relate to one another in addition to oneself (e.g., how do Sue and Dan get along with each other, and how do I get along with either of them?), which would allow perceivers to infer social latent group structure.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about what model might better capture social dynamics.

claim: If people represent social latent group structure in addition to dyadic similarities, then even when two agents' choices are equally similar to their own, the presence of a third agent altering the group structure should influence their decisions.
source: If people represent social latent group structure (Figure 1A) in addition to dyadic similarities, then even when two agents' choices (Agents A's and B's) are equally similar to their own, the presence of a third agent (Agent C) altering the group structure should influence their decisions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the latent structure learning model, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Dyadic similarity accounts would not predict differential ally-choice behavior when similarity is equated for the two agents in question.
source: Importantly, dyadic similarity accounts would not predict differential ally-choice behavior in these cases (because similarity is equated for the two agents in question).
evidence: This is a logical inference about what dyadic similarity models would predict.

claim: The key difference between the dyadic similarity and latent structure models is whether or not the presence of the third agent can affect how the first two agents are perceived.
source: In other words, the key difference between the two models is whether or not the presence of the third agent can affect how the first two agents are perceived.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical distinction between the two models.

claim: Recent evidence suggests that implicit bias and behavioral discrimination along political party lines is now as potent as bias against racial out-groups.
source: We focused on political issues because recent evidence suggests that implicit bias and behavioral discrimination along political party lines is now as potent as bias against racial out-groups (Iyengar et al., 2012; Iyengar and Westwood, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Iyengar et al., 2012 and Iyengar and Westwood, 2015.

claim: 42 participants were scanned using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) as they completed the structure-learning task.
source: We scanned 42 participants using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) as they completed our structure-learning task.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and sample size.

claim: Each participant completed six runs.
source: Each participant completed six runs; each run comprised learning about three novel agents across eight political issues and then choosing to ally with one of two agents on an unknown, 'mystery' issue.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Each run comprised learning about three novel agents across eight political issues and then choosing to ally with one of two agents on an unknown, 'mystery' issue.
source: Each participant completed six runs; each run comprised learning about three novel agents across eight political issues and then choosing to ally with one of two agents on an unknown, 'mystery' issue.
evidence: This describes the structure of each experimental run.

claim: Each participant saw 48 political issues and learned about 18 novel agents in total.
source: Each participant saw 48 political issues and learned about 18 novel agents in total.
evidence: This describes the total number of stimuli each participant encountered.

claim: The fully saturated model with both main effects and the interaction term fit the data better than without the interaction term (χ2(1) = 7.246, p=0.007).
source: Likelihood-ratio tests indicated that the fully saturated model with both main effects and the interaction term fit the data better than without the interaction term (χ2(1) = 7.246, p=0.007).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (likelihood-ratio test).

claim: There is a significant positive effect of Agent B's agreement in predicting the likelihood of choosing Agent B in the ally-choice trial (b = 2.325, Wald's z = 4.099, 95% CI [1.284, 3.519], p<0.001).
source: As a simple dyadic similarity account would predict, the model indicated a significant positive effect of Agent B's agreement in predicting the likelihood of choosing Agent B in the ally-choice trial, b = 2.325, Wald's z = 4.099, 95% CI [1.284, 3.519], p<0.001.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There is a significant positive effect of Agent C's agreement in predicting the likelihood of choosing Agent B in the ally-choice trial (b = 1.322, Wald's z = 2.633, 95% CI [0.371, 2.349], p=0.008).
source: However, as predicted by the latent structure learning account, the model also indicated a significant positive effect of Agent C's agreement in predicting the likelihood of choosing Agent B in the ally-choice trial, b = 1.322, Wald's z = 2.633, 95% CI [0.371, 2.349], p=0.008 (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: There is a significant negative interaction between the agreements of Agent B and Agent C (b = −0.307, Wald's z = −2.588, 95% CI [−0.550,–0.082], p=0.010).
source: This was qualified by a significant negative interaction between the agreements of Agent B and Agent C, b = −0.307, Wald's z = −2.588, 95% CI [−0.550,–0.082], p=0.010.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Even when adjusting for Agent B's agreement with the participant, increasing Agent C's alignment with the participant made respondents more likely to choose Agent B on the ally-choice trial.
source: In other words, even when adjusting for Agent B's agreement with the participant, increasing Agent C's alignment with the participant made respondents more likely to choose Agent B on the ally-choice trial.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results presented.

claim: When Agent B agreed with the participant a majority of the time, the additional variance explained by Agent C's agreement decreased.
source: However, this result was expectably qualified by a weak interaction: when Agent B agreed with the participant a majority of the time, the additional variance explained by Agent C's agreement decreased.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the interaction effect found in the statistical analysis.

claim: A dyadic similarity model would not predict that the level of agreement with Agent C should matter for choosing on the ally-choice trial.
source: While a dyadic similarity model would not predict that the level of agreement with Agent C should matter for choosing on the ally-choice trial, the latent structure learning model does predict that Agent C's level of agreement with the participant should matter in whether or not participants choose Agent B on the ally-choice trial.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about what the dyadic similarity model would predict.

claim: The latent structure learning model predicts that Agent C's level of agreement with the participant should matter in whether or not participants choose Agent B on the ally-choice trial.
source: While a dyadic similarity model would not predict that the level of agreement with Agent C should matter for choosing on the ally-choice trial, the latent structure learning model does predict that Agent C's level of agreement with the participant should matter in whether or not participants choose Agent B on the ally-choice trial.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about what the latent structure learning model would predict.

claim: Any difference in choice behavior as a result of Agent C's level of agreement is inconsistent with the dyadic similarity account.
source: Indeed, any difference in choice behavior as a result of Agent C's level of agreement is already inconsistent with the dyadic similarity account.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be inconsistent with the dyadic similarity model.

claim: Disambiguation between dyadic similarity and latent structure learning accounts of ally-choice have been demonstrated previously with model simulations and behavioral studies.
source: Disambiguation between these two accounts of ally-choice have been demonstrated previously with model simulations and behavioral studies (Gershman et al., 2017; Lau et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Trial-by-trial dyadic similarity correlated with activity in the ventral medial prefrontal cortex/pregenual anterior cingulate (pgACC).
source: As predicted, trial-by-trial dyadic similarity correlated with activity in the ventral medial prefrontal cortex/pregenual anterior cingulate (pgACC; Figure 4, green).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The similarity-over-agents modulator identified clusters in the pgACC, bilateral temporoparietal junction, right superior temporal sulcus, and left supplementary motor area.
source: The similarity-over-agents modulator identified clusters in the pgACC, bilateral temporoparietal junction, right superior temporal sulcus, and left supplementary motor area (Figure 4, yellow).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The pgACC cluster from the similarity-over-agents parametric modulator encompassed the pgACC cluster found by the dyadic similarity modulator.
source: Perhaps unsurprisingly, the pgACC cluster from this parametric modulator encompassed the pgACC cluster found by the dyadic similarity modulator.
evidence: This is an observation about the spatial overlap of clusters from different analyses.

claim: The latent structure learning model parametric modulator identified only a cluster in right anterior insula (rAI) that extended into the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG pars orbitalis).
source: In contrast, the latent structure learning model parametric modulator identified only a cluster in right anterior insula (rAI) that extended into the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG pars orbitalis; Figure 4, red).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The rAI cluster identified by the latent structure learning model did not overlap with any of the clusters identified by the dyadic similarity and similarity-over-agents models.
source: This rAI cluster did not overlap with any of the clusters identified by the previous two models.
evidence: This is an observation about the spatial distinctness of the rAI cluster.

claim: The rAI cluster overlapped with a separately identified rAI cluster associated with non-social cluster assignment updating.
source: Of note, this rAI cluster overlapped with a separately identified rAI cluster associated with non-social cluster assignment updating (Tomov et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with a previous study cited.

claim: The rAI cluster overlapped with 44.7% of the rAI result from Tomov et al., 2018.
source: To provide a description of the similarity: our rAI overlapped with 44.7% of that rAI result (i.e., number of common voxels across both ROIs divided by total number of rAI voxels in Tomov et al., 2018; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of ROIs and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activity in the independently defined ROI from Tomov et al., 2018 correlated significantly with the latent group model (cluster-level FDR-corrected q = 0.014).
source: Activity in this independently defined ROI correlated significantly with our latent group model, cluster-level FDR-corrected q = 0.014.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The protected exceedance probability (PXP) in the rAI was 82.34% for the latent structure model, 6.44% for the dyadic similarity model, and 11.23% for the similarity-over-agents model.
source: The PXP in the rAI was 82.34% for the latent structure model, but only 6.44% for the dyadic similarity model and 11.23% for the similarity-over-agents model.
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian model selection analysis.

claim: The Bayesian omnibus risk (BOR) for the rAI was 0.190.
source: The BOR was 0.190.
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian model selection analysis.

claim: The latent structure model explained significant variance in the rAI.
source: In sum, the latent structure model explained significant variance in the rAI.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PXP and BOR results.

claim: The BOR for the pgACC was 0.675.
source: The BOR was 0.675.
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian model selection analysis.

claim: For the pgACC, no single model was especially frequent over the other two.
source: In other words, for the pgACC, no single model was especially frequent over the other two.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PXP and BOR results for pgACC.

claim: Adding the signal from the rAI cluster helped to better predict variability in choice behavior for the latent structure model (χ2(1) = 5.312, p=0.021).
source: While a likelihood ratio test showed that adding the signal from the rAI cluster helped to better predict variability in choice behavior for the latent structure model (χ2(1) = 5.312, p=0.021), neither the addition of the signal from the pgACC to the dyadic similarity model (χ2(1) = 1.526, p=0.217), nor the addition of signal from any of the clusters associated with the similarity-over-agents model helped improve predictions of choice variability (χ2(1)s < 2.112, ps >0.250).
evidence: This claim is supported by likelihood ratio test of behavioral prediction models.

claim: The addition of the signal from the pgACC to the dyadic similarity model did not help improve predictions of choice variability (χ2(1) = 1.526, p=0.217).
source: While a likelihood ratio test showed that adding the signal from the rAI cluster helped to better predict variability in choice behavior for the latent structure model (χ2(1) = 5.312, p=0.021), neither the addition of the signal from the pgACC to the dyadic similarity model (χ2(1) = 1.526, p=0.217), nor the addition of signal from any of the clusters associated with the similarity-over-agents model helped improve predictions of choice variability (χ2(1)s < 2.112, ps >0.250).
evidence: This claim is supported by likelihood ratio test of behavioral prediction models.

claim: The addition of signal from any of the clusters associated with the similarity-over-agents model did not help improve predictions of choice variability (χ2(1)s < 2.112, ps >0.250).
source: While a likelihood ratio test showed that adding the signal from the rAI cluster helped to better predict variability in choice behavior for the latent structure model (χ2(1) = 5.312, p=0.021), neither the addition of the signal from the pgACC to the dyadic similarity model (χ2(1) = 1.526, p=0.217), nor the addition of signal from any of the clusters associated with the similarity-over-agents model helped improve predictions of choice variability (χ2(1)s < 2.112, ps >0.250).
evidence: This claim is supported by likelihood ratio test of behavioral prediction models.

claim: This is the only evidence of which we are aware that pgACC supports incremental revisions of representations of similarity between oneself and others, both directly and across third agents.
source: First, this is the only evidence of which we are aware that pgACC supports incremental revisions of representations of similarity between oneself and others, both directly and across third agents.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding relative to existing literature.

claim: Using novel agents allowed examination of how participants' degree of alignment changed as they learned agents' preferences over time.
source: In contrast to research that relies on preexisting knowledge about specific groups or individuals, using novel agents allowed us to examine how participants' degree of alignment changed as they learned agents' preferences over time.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological advantage of the experimental design.

claim: The rAI result is consistent with previous work on updating of non-social latent structure.
source: Second, our rAI result is consistent with previous work on updating of non-social latent structure (Tomov et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with a cited previous study.

claim: Social categorization is distinct from other forms of categorization because it requires participants to categorize themselves.
source: Note, though, that social categorization is distinct from other forms of categorization because it requires participants to categorize themselves (Turner et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Turner et al., 1987.

claim: The results demonstrate that rAI is capable of learning egocentrically defined latent structures.
source: Thus, our results demonstrate that rAI is capable of learning egocentrically defined latent structures.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in light of the distinction between social and non-social categorization.

claim: Connectivity of the anterior insula with the anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala, and ventral tegmental area (a 'salience detection' network) and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (associated with cognitive control) likely affords the flexibility required to represent context-specific coalition members.
source: Connectivity of the anterior insula with the anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala, and ventral tegmental area (a 'salience detection' network; Seeley et al., 2007) and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (associated with cognitive control; Chang et al., 2013) likely affords the flexibility required to represent context-specific coalition members—someone who may be a coalition member at a debate may not be a fellow coalition member at a sports event.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations about brain connectivity and involves speculation about functional implications.

claim: AI is heavily involved in socially-relevant computations, including but not limited to self-awareness tasks such as awareness of emotions and subjective pain.
source: AI is also heavily involved in socially-relevant computations, including but not limited to self-awareness tasks such as awareness of emotions and subjective pain, and exhibits hypoactivity in persons with autism spectrum disorder on tasks such as face processing and theory of mind (Uddin and Menon, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Uddin and Menon, 2009.

claim: AI exhibits hypoactivity in persons with autism spectrum disorder on tasks such as face processing and theory of mind.
source: AI is also heavily involved in socially-relevant computations, including but not limited to self-awareness tasks such as awareness of emotions and subjective pain, and exhibits hypoactivity in persons with autism spectrum disorder on tasks such as face processing and theory of mind (Uddin and Menon, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Uddin and Menon, 2009.

claim: The rAI region identified included a part of the IFG (specifically, pars orbitalis).
source: The rAI region we identified included a part of the IFG (specifically, pars orbitalis).
evidence: This is a description of the anatomical extent of the identified cluster.

claim: In studies of hierarchical processing in music and language, the IFG pars orbitalis has been associated with sentence comprehension.
source: In studies of hierarchical processing in music and language, this area has been associated with sentence comprehension (Silbert et al., 2014) and found to exhibit sensitivity to violations of hierarchical regularities (Cheung et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The IFG pars orbitalis exhibits sensitivity to violations of hierarchical regularities.
source: In studies of hierarchical processing in music and language, this area has been associated with sentence comprehension (Silbert et al., 2014) and found to exhibit sensitivity to violations of hierarchical regularities (Cheung et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cheung et al., 2018.

claim: The IFG is involved in building up sentence structure and meaning as semantic information is processed.
source: This area is also involved in building up sentence structure and meaning as semantic information is processed (Jeon and Friederici, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jeon and Friederici, 2013.

claim: The IFG has been hypothesized to represent individual episodes for later recombination.
source: Additionally, the IFG has been hypothesized to represent individual episodes for later recombination (Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013.

claim: The IFG may be recruited to build up inferences of social latent structures as participants learn more about other agents' preferences.
source: Just as this area may be recruited to build up the structures of sentences and tonal patterns, it may also be building up inferences of social latent structures as participants learn more about other agents' preferences.
evidence: This is a speculative claim drawing an analogy between linguistic/musical processing and social structure learning.

claim: The brain tracks both dyadic similarity and latent structure alignment signals.
source: Finally, it is worth noting that while the brain tracks both of these alignment signals, variability in the signal from only one of the regions, rAI, helped improve model predictions of behavioral choices.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: It is possible that had participants been asked to make a different choice (e.g., identify which agent better represented a particular trait), the pgACC signal may have been more relevant.
source: It is possible that had participants been asked to make a different choice (e.g., identify which agent better represented a particular trait), the pgACC signal may have been more relevant.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about alternative experimental conditions.

source: From our 333 participants, we recruited 61 right-handed participants (48 female, Mage = 21.74 years, SD = 4.17) in order to achieve a sample size of at least 40 participants after exclusions.

claim: The target sample size was at least 40 participants after exclusions.

source: This sample size was determined based on sample sizes used in other fMRI experiments (e.g., Tomov et al., 2018; Cheung et al., 2018).

claim: Two participants requested to be removed from the scanner prior to the end of the study.
source: Two participants requested to be removed from the scanner prior to the end of the study, and two participants were excluded due to a computer crash, resulting in unrecorded responses.
evidence: This describes participant attrition.

claim: Two participants were excluded due to a computer crash, resulting in unrecorded responses.
source: Two participants requested to be removed from the scanner prior to the end of the study, and two participants were excluded due to a computer crash, resulting in unrecorded responses.
evidence: This describes participant exclusion due to technical issues.

claim: Eight participants were excluded for excessive head movements of 4 mm or more.
source: Prior to any data analysis, we excluded five participants who fell asleep in the scanner, eight participants for excessive head movements of 4 mm or more, one participant who correctly deduced the hypothesis of the study, and one participant for missing at least one self-response per run.

claim: One participant was excluded who correctly deduced the hypothesis of the study.

claim: One participant was excluded for missing at least one self-response per run.

claim: The final sample size was 42 participants (32 female, Mage = 22.07 years, SD = 4.82).
source: This left us with a sample size of 42 participants (32 female, Mage = 22.07 years, SD = 4.82).
evidence: This describes the final analyzed sample.

claim: Participants provided informed consent to participate and consent to publish.
source: Participants provided informed consent to participate and consent to publish; all procedures complied with Harvard University's Committee on the Use of Human Subjects' guidelines (Protocol #IRB15-2048).
evidence: This describes ethical procedures followed.

claim: All procedures complied with Harvard University's Committee on the Use of Human Subjects' guidelines (Protocol #IRB15-2048).
source: Participants provided informed consent to participate and consent to publish; all procedures complied with Harvard University's Committee on the Use of Human Subjects' guidelines (Protocol #IRB15-2048).
evidence: This describes ethical approval for the study.

claim: Political issues were selected from ISideWith.com that had accumulated at least 500,000 votes and had the greatest agreement/disagreement discrepancies.
source: We selected issues that had accumulated at least 500,000 votes and had the greatest agreement/disagreement discrepancies, as described in Experiment 2 in Lau et al. (2018).
evidence: This describes the stimulus selection criteria.

claim: 48 issues with the lowest yes-no differences as of May 2017 were included in the main task.
source: We included the 48 issues with the lowest yes-no differences as of May 2017 in the main task (see OSF for complete materials).
evidence: This describes the final stimulus set used.

claim: A total of 36 photos were selected from the Chicago Face Database (CFD) and gender-matched to the participant.
source: For agent pictures, we selected a total of 36 photos from the Chicago Face Database (CFD; Ma et al., 2015) and gender-matched agents to the participant.
evidence: This describes the face stimuli selection procedure.

claim: The pool of 'White' faces was extracted based on CFD designations.
source: We extracted the pool of 'White' faces (based on CFD designations) and eliminated faces based on the norming data provided by the CFD until 18 female and 18 male faces were left.
evidence: This describes the face selection process.

claim: The order of presentation of the 48 issues as well as the sides on which the agreement positions appeared on the screen were randomized for each participant.
source: The order of presentation of the 48 issues as well as the sides on which the agreement positions appeared on the screen were randomized for each participant.
evidence: This describes the randomization procedure.

claim: Participants had 4.5 s to choose whether they would support a political issue.
source: They then had 4.5 s to choose whether they would support that issue; a gray rectangle appeared around their selection when they had made their choice.

claim: Agents were gender-matched to participants' self-reported gender and only White faces were used to avoid participants weighting information from agents who looked more similar to them.
source: To avoid participants weighting information from agents who looked more similar to them, we gender-matched the agents to participants' self-reported gender and only used White faces.
evidence: This describes the rationale for stimulus selection decisions.

claim: Participants had 4.5 s to guess an agent's preference.
source: Participants first saw a picture of one of the agents alongside his/her name and were asked to predict the preference of that agent with regards to the issue (e.g., 'Which do you think Annie chose?'); each participant had 4.5 s to guess, and a gray rectangle appeared around their selection after they made a choice.
evidence: This describes the timing of the experimental task.

claim: Between each screen, a fixation cross appeared for 3 s-16 s (jittered).
source: Between each screen, a fixation cross appeared for 3 s-16 s (jittered).
evidence: This describes the timing of the experimental task.

claim: Jitter was generated using the optseq algorithm.
source: Jitter was generated using the optseq algorithm (http://www.surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/optseq).
evidence: This describes the method for generating jittered timing.

claim: A table consisting of eight rows and four columns displayed on the right-hand side of the screen recorded the participant's and each Agent's responses on each trial.
source: A table consisting of eight rows and four columns displayed on the right-hand side of the screen recorded the participant's and each Agent's responses on each trial.
evidence: This describes a feature of the experimental interface.

claim: The order of the policy positions and agents was randomized.
source: The order of the policy positions and agents was randomized; every participant saw each of the 48 policies and 18 agents only once during the experiment.
evidence: This describes the randomization procedure.

claim: Every participant saw each of the 48 policies and 18 agents only once during the experiment.
source: The order of the policy positions and agents was randomized; every participant saw each of the 48 policies and 18 agents only once during the experiment.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The order of the agents was randomized across runs.
source: The order of the agents was also randomized across runs.
evidence: This describes the randomization procedure.

claim: Agents were randomly assigned names from a preset list of names of five-letter length.
source: Agents were randomly assigned names from a preset list of names of five-letter length.
evidence: This describes how agent names were assigned.

claim: For each run, Agents B and C agreed on five issues.
source: For each run, Agents B and C agreed on five issues; Agents A and C agreed on three issues, and Agents A and B never agreed with each other.
evidence: This describes the agreement structure built into the experimental design.

claim: For each run, Agents A and C agreed on three issues.
source: For each run, Agents B and C agreed on five issues; Agents A and C agreed on three issues, and Agents A and B never agreed with each other.
